newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Top Philippine tycoon once considered art trade.
newsitem.headline: Top Philippine tycoon once considered art trade.

text.p: He once flirted with the idea of becoming an art auctioneer, but Jaime Augusto Zobel de Ayala is now set on guiding the family-controlled Ayala group, one of the richest conglomerates in the Philippines, into the 21st century.

Ayala, 37, belongs to the seventh generation of a family descended from Spanish landowners who settled in the Philippines. He took over last year as president of Ayala Corp, the flagship of a group that traces its roots to a distillery set up in Manila in 1834.

Today, it is one of the most famous names in Philippine business, with interests stretching from massive real estate holdings in the Makati commercial district of the capital to banking, food, transportation, telecommunications and insurance.

"We see ourselves as a company with a strong value system...a company that believes in doing things with a strong ethical standard," Jaime Ayala told Reuters in an interview on Monday in Ayala Tower, a landmark high-rise that also houses the Philippine Stock Exchange.

"These value systems I believe are really my responsibility to continue...and keep as a part of the way we do business as we grow and as we become more aggressive from a corporate point of view," he said.

Ayala said he spent many of his early years in Britain, where his father was the Philippine ambassador. After receiving a degree at Harvard he was entranced by the world of art, but even there his business instincts surfaced.
"I almost did a thesis on the art auction business. I was quite fascinated by that mix of art and business and almost joined a training programme at Sotheby's," he said.
His father, "Don" Jaime Zobel de Ayala, who was then president of the group, persuaded him to work in the family business for three years, and Ayala said he was hooked.
"I fell in love with Asia again and everything out here. There's been no turning back since," he said.
Now Ayala sees himself at the helm of the group until he retires at 60, and has plans to diversify into non-traditional areas and increase synergy between the various subsidiaries.
"What I would like to bring is a certain urgency to the way we do things, really move a lot quicker to take advantage of some of the opportunities that are opening up around us," he said.
"We have traditionally been known as a conservative company and a financially prudent one. I would not want to change that image in any way, particularly the financially prudent one.
"However, I believe as a conglomerate there is a lot more we can do in terms of finding ways to create synergy between our group companies. It's a different way of doing things," he said.
Ayala also intends to seek new growth areas other than the group's traditional dependence on real estate and banking.
"Those we will continue to grow at a very strong pace. However, we will be moving into new areas -- telecommunications is one major area we are working on right now," he said.

"We will be in infrastructure, maybe the transportation side, in a more visible way," Ayala said. "These are all new areas for us that are really very much a cornerstone of the kind of services that are needed in the next century."
One thing Ayala said he would not forget is his responsibility to his family and the group's future, and what he described as its destiny to be intertwined with the future of the Philippines.
"We see ourselves not just as a profit centre that is good for investments. We really like to remain very much aligned to the national development efforts of the government," he said.
"We are very much a part of the Philippines, and certainly our family is very attached and proud of our association with Ayala," he said.
"That responsibility that we have over the company and in maintaining it for future generations is something that both my father and I hold very dear and consider very important."
